title: Present simple: positive statements
objectives: Use the present simple to describe routines and general facts.
Choose the correct verb form for singular and plural subjects.
Spell common third-person singular verb forms.

explanation.heading: Meaning and use
paragraphs: We use the present simple to talk about habits and routines: things that happen regularly. It also describes facts and situations that are generally true. ‘I walk to college’ describes a routine; it does not mean I am walking at this exact moment. ‘Water boils at 100°C’ describes a general fact under normal pressure.

A subject is the person or thing that does an action. In a positive statement, the subject normally comes before the main verb: ‘They play tennis.’ In this unit we practise positive statements. Present simple questions and negatives are taught in the next unit. The verb be has a different pattern, which you studied in Unit 1.

explanation.heading: Form
paragraphs: With I, you, we and they, use the base form of the verb: ‘I work’, ‘you study’, ‘we live’ and ‘they play’. With he, she or it, usually add -s: ‘he works’, ‘she lives’ and ‘it rains’. Use the same -s form with one person’s name or one singular thing: ‘Aisha works’ and ‘the bus stops’.

Some verbs have a spelling change. Add -es to verbs ending in -s, -sh, -ch, -x or -o: ‘passes’, ‘washes’, ‘watches’, ‘fixes’ and ‘goes’. When a verb ends in a consonant plus y, change y to i and add -es: ‘study’ becomes ‘studies’. After a vowel plus y, add only -s: ‘play’ becomes ‘plays’. Have is irregular: ‘he has’.

explanation.heading: Examples in context
paragraphs: Time expressions often help show a routine. We can say ‘every day’, ‘on Mondays’, ‘at weekends’ or ‘in the morning’. They often appear at the end of a sentence. They describe how often or when something happens; the verb must still agree with the subject.

Look at the examples below. In ‘My friends live nearby’, friends means more than one person, so use live. In ‘My friend lives nearby’, friend means one person, so use lives. You refers to one person or several people, but the verb stays the same: ‘You work’.

explanation.heading: Contrasts and common mistakes
paragraphs: Do not add -s after I, you, we or they: ‘They work’ is correct. Do not forget -s, -es or the spelling change after he, she or it in a positive present simple sentence. Do not add a form of be before an ordinary main verb in this structure: ‘She works here’, not ‘She is works here’.

The present simple can describe a regular situation even if it is not happening now. ‘He works in a café’ can be true when he is at home. A different form, the present continuous, is often used for an action happening now; you will study it later. First choose the subject, then check the verb ending.

examples.sentence: I walk to college every morning.
examples.note: I takes the base form walk.

examples.sentence: My sister works in a café.

examples.note: We takes the base form study.
After a consonant, y changes to ies.
After a vowel, add s to play.

examples.sentence: The bus goes to the station.
examples.note: Go becomes goes with a singular subject.

examples.sentence: My neighbours watch films on Saturdays.
examples.note: The plural subject takes the base form watch.

examples.sentence: Our teacher has a small garden.
examples.note: Have changes to has with a singular subject.

common_errors.reason: Add s to work after she.
Use the base form after they.
Do not put is before the present simple main verb plays.

summary: Use the present simple for routines and general facts.
Use the base verb with I, you, we and they; use a third-person singular form with he, she and it.
Check spelling changes such as watches, studies, goes and has.
